# Find a file, a line, or a directory

> The finder in the shell, telescope in the editor, and ripgrep underneath.

One key opens everything: `F3` asks what you are looking for, then which channel to look in — files, directories, file contents, git log, the manual, history — and opens that channel with your query already typed. Pick a row and it opens in a new pane below you. It is a tmux binding, so it answers from inside the editor and inside an agent pane too; in the editor telescope remains a second finder, deliberately not unified with this one.

## `F3`

**Search: say what, then pick the channel**

*terminal*

Press `F3` in any pane — a shell, an editor, a running agent — and a one-line box titled `search` opens. Type what you are looking for and press enter; the channel list opens, and whichever channel you pick opens with your query already typed into its row list. Pick a row and it acts exactly as `F8` does: files and matches open in the editor below your pane, a directory opens a shell there, anything else lands on a fresh prompt unrun. Esc at any step leaves nothing behind. To search your whole machine, `cd ~` first.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> It is `F8` with the query first — one script (`tv-go find`), and the channels under `~/.config/television/cable` are the only list of places to search. It replaced `tv-all`, a 456-line second copy of those channels that counted hits per channel and ran a background scan of `$HOME`; the counts cost a hand-written lane per channel, and `$HOME` needed a cache, a second ignore list and a reaper. It is a tmux binding rather than a reedline one so that it fires inside nvim and inside an agent pane; the query comes from tmux's own `command-prompt`, whose Escape cancels silently. The popup is drawn with `-B` because television draws its own frame and a tmux border one cell outside it tears on every redraw.

See also: [`F8`](./files.md#f8) · [`finder`](./files.md#finder) · [`Ctrl-Q`](./history.md#ctrl-q)

## `finder`

**Run a picker and get typed nushell data back**

*shell*

`finder` opens the channel remote; `finder --start files` opens one channel directly. The return value is data, not a string: a list of paths, `{file, line, text}` rows from a grep, `{hash}` records from `git-log`. Pipe it like anything else.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> Typed decode per channel is what lets one opener do the right thing for a file, a directory, a grep hit and a commit — and it is why new pickers are new channels plus a decode, never a new hand-rolled TUI.

See also: [`F3`](./files.md#f3) · [`tv channel`](./files.md#tv-channel)

## `F8`

**Pick a channel, then a row, and act on it**

*terminal*

Press `F8` in any pane and a list of channels opens over it. Type until one is left and it opens by itself (or press `Enter`), then pick a row: a file or a text match opens in the editor below your pane, a directory opens a shell there, a commit is shown, a history line lands on a fresh prompt unrun. The `theme` and `font` channels preview live over the whole terminal and `Enter` keeps the pick. Any other channel types its row into your pane.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> F3 is the same two steps with the query typed first. The font channel lives only here: the font is WezTerm's, so a pick is written to `~/.local/state/wezterm/font.txt`, which the WezTerm config watches, and the live preview is a user variable WezTerm turns into a per-window override. The channel step and the theme and font pickers run in fzf, not television: television 0.15.9 only auto-accepts a single entry at startup and caches each row's preview, so going back to a row would not repaint. fzf's `one:accept` and its per-focus preview do both.

See also: [`F7`](./files.md#f7) · [`F3`](./files.md#f3) · [`F9`](./appearance.md#f9)

## `grep`

**Search file contents with ripgrep**

*shell*

`grep <pattern>` is `rg <pattern>` — recursive by default, respecting ignore files. Reach for `rg` and `fd`, not `grep` and `find`.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> `rg` and `fd` share one ignore ruleset through `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, so a path hidden from one is hidden from both.

See also: [`F3`](./files.md#f3) · [`idioms`](./agents.md#idioms)

## `F7`

**Pick a channel, then a row, and type it into this pane**

*terminal*

Same two steps as `F8`, but whatever you pick is typed into the pane you pressed `F7` in, unrun — a path, a commit hash, a branch, a history line.

See also: [`F8`](./files.md#f8)

## Understand what a channel is, and add one

*shell*

Nothing to run. A channel is a cable file under `~/.config/television` naming a source command that emits rows, plus how to preview one. Add a file and `tv <name>` and `finder --start <name>` reach it immediately; teach `finder` how to decode its rows and every opener works on it too. `F3` and `F8` list it at once; `tv-go` decides what picking one of its rows does, and anything it does not know lands on a fresh prompt unrun.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> One rule keeps the picker surface from sprawling: television owns every picker screen. The curated set is files, dirs, text, zoxide, env, quicklist, git-log, git-files, git-branch, recent dirs (`recent-dirs`, fed by the dirstack), recent files, alias, `nu-history` and `docs` (every line of the manual's prose, opened in the editor at the hit), plus the `theme` channel behind the scheme picker — anything else migrates on demand. The rule has exactly one exception, and it is named rather than tolerated: `zi` reaches fzf through `zoxide query --interactive`. A second picker outside tv would be a new decision, not an appeal to that one. tv runs on the `default` ANSI theme so it inherits the terminal's palette instead of baking hex values.

See also: [`finder`](./files.md#finder) · [`F3`](./files.md#f3)

## `<leader>ff and <leader><space>`

**Find files in the project**

*nvim normal*

Either one opens telescope over the project's files; type any part of the path. `<leader><space>` exists because it is the fastest thing your thumb can do.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> This is the editor's finder, and it is deliberately not the shell's. television owns the shell's pickers, telescope owns the editor's; unifying them was considered and rejected.

See also: [`<Tab> <S-Tab> <CR> (telescope)`](./files.md#tab-s-tab-cr-telescope) · [`<leader>fg`](./files.md#leader-fg)

## `<leader>fg`

**Grep the project live**

*nvim normal*

Press `<leader>fg`, then type: the search runs over file contents as you type, and enter opens the file on the matching line.

See also: [`<leader>ff and <leader><space>`](./files.md#leader-ff-and-leader-space) · [`<Tab> <S-Tab> <CR> (telescope)`](./files.md#tab-s-tab-cr-telescope)

## `<leader>fb`

**Switch to an open buffer**

*nvim normal*

Press `<leader>fb` to get the open buffers as a picker, then type part of a name and press enter — the alternative to walking them with `H` and `L` when there are many.

See also: [`<S-h> <S-l> <leader>bd`](./editing.md#s-h-s-l-leader-bd)

## `<leader>fh`

**Search Neovim's own help**

*nvim normal*

Press `<leader>fh`, then type a topic: it fuzzy-searches the help tags — vim's documentation, not this manual. `help` in the shell is this configuration; `:help` in the editor is Neovim.

## `<Tab> <S-Tab> <CR> (telescope)`

**Send several picks to the quickfix list**

*nvim normal*

Inside any telescope picker, `<Tab>` marks the highlighted row and steps one entry towards the worse matches, `<S-Tab>` marks and steps back towards the better ones — the best match sits at the bottom next to the prompt, so `<Tab>` walks up the screen. Then `<CR>`: with anything marked it sends every mark to the quickfix list and opens it; with nothing marked it just opens the highlighted row. The same keys work whether you are typing or in normal mode inside the picker.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> `prose` because these maps are buffer-local to telescope's own prompt buffer, created only while a picker is open and gone once it closes — `maparg` can see them (a live picker really does return an `lhs`, with `buffer = 1`), but nothing static can, so no `nvim --headless` probe outside a running picker has anything to check against.

See also: [`<leader>fg`](./files.md#leader-fg)

## `<leader>e`

**Open the current directory as a buffer**

*nvim normal*

Press `<leader>e` in any buffer: oil opens on the directory of the current file, dotfiles included. It is a normal buffer — rename a line, delete a line, add a line, then `:w` and the filesystem matches.

> **Why it is this way**
>
> `<leader>e` is the fast path, not the only one: oil loads eagerly (`lazy = false`) so its `default_file_explorer` hijack is installed at startup, and `:e some/dir` reaches it with no key pressed. Netrw is disabled either way, so nothing else could claim the directory instead.
